en.title: Lost Dog: What to Do Right Now to Find Them
en.metaDesc: Lost your dog? Here's how to find a lost dog step by step: search nearby, alert shelters and vets, check the microchip, and post an alert on Orma.
en.html:
If your dog has just gone missing, your heart is probably racing, so take a breath: the first few hours really matter, and staying calm makes a difference. A lost dog often stays close to where it wandered off, so every minute you use well improves your chances of a happy reunion. This guide walks you through what to do right now, step by step, so you know exactly how to find a lost dog without wasting precious time.

Act right away: the first hours matter most

The moment you realise your dog is gone, don't wait. Many dogs are found in the first few hours, close to where they slipped away. Before you head out, grab a few things that can help.

  • A recent, clear photo of your dog showing coat, size and any distinctive markings.
  • The lead, some treats and maybe a favourite toy or a blanket with your dog's scent.
  • The microchip number, if you have it, and your vet's contact details.

Search nearby and call in a calm voice

Go back to the spot where you last saw your dog and widen the search on foot. Call your dog gently, not in a panicked shout: an anxious tone can frighten a scared dog and make it hide even more.

  • Check hedges, bushes, gardens, open garages and shady corners where a frightened dog might take shelter.
  • Search especially at dawn and dusk, when there is less noise and traffic.
  • Ask everyone you meet (passers-by, shopkeepers, other dog walkers) if they've seen your dog, and leave your number.

Alert shelters, vets and local authorities

People who find a dog often take it to the nearest vet or report it to a shelter. Making yourself easy to reach across these channels is key to getting your dog back.

  • Contact your local animal shelters and pounds, leaving a description and your contact details.
  • Notify nearby veterinary practices: if someone brings in a found dog, they can link it to your report.
  • In Italy, if the dog is in danger (on a road, injured), you can call 112 or the Forestry Carabinieri on 1515.

Check the microchip and your registered details

A microchip is the most reliable way for anyone to trace a found dog back to you, but only if your details are current. Now is the moment to make sure they are.

  • Ask your vet to confirm the microchip is registered with the correct, up-to-date contact number.
  • If you've changed your phone number or address, update them straight away: outdated details make the chip useless.
  • Anyone who finds your dog and takes it to a vet or shelter can scan the chip and reach you.

Flyers, social media and local groups

The more people who know you're searching, the more eyes are looking for you. A clear flyer and the right channels multiply your chances.

  • Make a simple flyer with a big photo, the area where your dog went missing, your phone number and a note saying "don't chase, please call me".
  • Put it up near the spot, in shops, at vets and on neighbourhood boards.
  • Post in local lost-and-found pet groups on Facebook and ask people to share.

Post an alert on Orma to reach nearby neighbours

Orma is a community app for missing pets, built for exactly this moment when the search needs to be fast and reach everyone around you. You can create a report in a few taps and instantly let the people nearby know you're searching.

  • People near you get an automatic alert when something moves, so many extra eyes join the search right away.
  • If someone spots your dog, they can add a photo and location, so you recognise your dog at a glance and know where to focus.
  • If a found dog shares your dog's microchip, the match happens automatically; chat stays inside the app so your contact details stay private, and pet locations on the map are blurred for safety.

I know this is a hard moment, but you're not alone and it's far from hopeless: a great many dogs are found, often within hours or a few days of going missing. Keep searching calmly, keep every channel open, and let the network of people around you help. There's a real chance you'll be holding your friend again soon.

faqEn.q: My dog went missing a few hours ago: what should I do first?
faqEn.a: Go back to the last place you saw your dog and call out calmly: frightened dogs often stay hidden nearby. Report the loss right away on Orma with a photo and location, so people in the area get an alert and can help you look.

faqEn.q: Do lost dogs find their way back home on their own?
faqEn.a: It can happen, especially close to home and in the first few hours. Don't count on it, though: leave their bed or a worn piece of your clothing outside so your scent is there, keep an entrance open if you can, and keep searching and spreading the word in the meantime.

faqEn.q: Who should I notify when my dog is lost?
faqEn.a: Contact your local shelter and, in Italy, the veterinary service of the ASL, since that's where found animals are usually taken. If your dog has a microchip, the pet registry lets people trace the dog back to you when a vet scans it.

faqEn.q: How can I quickly let my whole neighborhood know my dog is lost?
faqEn.a: With Orma you post the missing report in a few taps and nearby people get an alert; if someone spots your dog they can send you a photo and location. The app also creates a PDF flyer with a QR code you can print or share in local groups.

en.title: Lost Cat: How to Find a Lost Cat and Bring It Home
en.metaDesc: Lost your cat? Here's a calm, practical guide on how to find a lost cat: where and when to search, scent lures, microchips and who to alert nearby.
en.html:
If you've just realised your cat is gone, take a breath: the reassuring truth is that a lost cat usually doesn't go far. Unlike dogs, frightened cats tend to hide silently very close to home, sometimes just a few metres away, staying still for hours or days. This guide walks you through how to find a lost cat, calmly and step by step: where to look, when, which lures actually work, and who to tell.

Why a lost cat hides close to home

Understanding how cats behave helps you search in the right places. A cat that is scared or disorientated goes into survival mode: it tucks itself into a quiet hiding spot and stays put, often without answering when you call. It isn't ignoring you, it's simply frightened. That's why walking around calling loudly often fails: your cat is closer than you think, but keeping quiet.

  • Indoor cats rarely stray beyond a few gardens, so focus your search within the first 50-100 metres.
  • Cats used to going outside may roam wider, but they usually stick to familiar routes.
  • In the first 24-48 hours they tend to stay frozen in place, so patience matters more than distance.

Search at night and at dawn, when it's quiet

The best time to look for a lost cat is late at night or in the early hours of dawn, when there's little noise and traffic. Your cat feels safer moving around, and you can hear it more easily.

  • Move slowly and quietly, stopping often to listen for a faint meow or rustle.
  • Use a torch and sweep it slowly under cars, hedges and dark corners: a cat's eyes reflect light, so you'll see them shine in the dark.
  • Call in your normal, calm voice, then stay silent and listen for a full minute before moving on.

Check every hiding spot, one by one

A frightened cat looks for tight, dark, sheltered places. Patiently check every possible hiding spot, even the ones that seem unlikely.

  • Under cars, in stairwells, garages, cellars and storage rooms.
  • Under thick hedges, wood piles, stacked materials and large plant pots.
  • Politely ask neighbours to check sheds, garages and outbuildings: a cat can easily get shut inside by mistake.
  • Look up too: cats sometimes climb trees or roofs and can't get back down.

Use scents your cat recognises

A cat's sense of smell is extraordinary, so use it to guide them home. Familiar scents are a far stronger lure than any food.

  • Place your cat's used litter tray outside the door: its own scent helps it find the way back.
  • Leave a bowl of its usual food or something strong-smelling, along with its blanket or bed.
  • If you can, keep a low window or door open at night, as many cats slip back in once everything is calm.
  • Avoid leaving lots of food out overnight so you don't attract other animals: small amounts in the right spots are enough.

Alert neighbours, vets and shelters

The more people looking, the sooner you'll find your cat. Spread the word locally in a simple, organised way.

  • Tell neighbours in person or in local groups, sharing a clear, recent photo.
  • Call nearby vets and clinics: whoever finds a cat often takes it there to scan for a microchip.
  • Contact your local shelter and municipal animal services, as stray or found animals usually pass through them.
  • If your cat has a microchip, make sure your contact details on the pet registry are up to date; a vet can check this for you.
  • If you see any animal injured or in danger, contact your local emergency or animal welfare services.

Report it on Orma and get help from people nearby

While you search, report your lost cat on Orma, the app for missing pets. In just a few taps you automatically alert people near you, so many local eyes start looking at the same moment. Anyone who spots a similar cat can post a sighting with a photo and location, and you'll recognise your cat straight away. If someone finds a cat with a microchip, the automatic matching can link it to your report, and the chat stays inside the app so your contact details remain protected while you coordinate.

Finding a cat often takes patience: many come back after several days, once the fear fades. Keep searching during the quiet hours, leave familiar scents near your home, and keep your reports up to date. You're not alone in this search, and every small step brings the moment your friend returns a little closer.

faqEn.q: How many days does it take for a lost cat to come home?
faqEn.a: Many cats come back on their own within a few days, often at night when things are quiet. House cats usually hide close to home, typically within a few hundred metres, so it's worth searching nearby for a good while.

faqEn.q: Where does a cat hide when it runs away from home?
faqEn.a: Usually very close by: under cars, in cellars, garages, hedges, sheds or tight spaces where it feels safe. Check these spots early in the morning and after sunset, when cats move around more, and call your cat in a calm voice.

faqEn.q: How can I get my lost cat to come back?
faqEn.a: Put its litter box, a blanket or your worn clothes outside: familiar smells help it find its way. Leave out a bowl of food, go out during quiet hours calling softly, and if you can, ask neighbours to check their garages and cellars.

faqEn.q: What should I do if my microchipped cat is lost?
faqEn.a: Report the loss to your local veterinary health authority and make sure your contact details in the pet registry are up to date, so anyone who takes your cat to a vet or shelter can trace you. With Orma you can also post the report, and the microchip enables an automatic match if someone finds your cat.

en.title: I Found an Animal: What to Do, Step by Step
en.metaDesc: Found a dog or a cat and not sure what to do? A calm, practical guide to keeping the animal safe, checking the microchip and finding the owner.
en.html:
If you've just found an animal and don't know what to do, take a breath: you've already done the most important thing by stopping to help. Whether you've found a dog wandering near a road or a frightened cat in your garden, the steps are simple and they all point to one goal: getting them back to whoever is looking for them. Here's what to do, in the right order, without rushing and without forcing anything.

Keep the animal you found safe, without forcing it

A lost animal is often scared and can react unpredictably, even if it's usually gentle. When you've found an animal, the first rule is to approach calmly, without chasing it or backing it into a corner.

  • Speak in a low, steady voice and move slowly.
  • If it's a dog, try offering water and, if you have one, a lead or a piece of rope to keep it away from traffic.
  • If it's a cat, don't force contact: let it come to you. An open carrier or box helps.
  • Don't handle an animal that looks aggressive or is in real panic: wait, or ask for help.

If it's injured or in danger, get help right away

The animal's health comes first. If you find it hurt, hit by a car or clearly in distress, don't wait.

  • Contact a vet or your local public veterinary service as soon as possible.
  • For an animal in serious danger, in Italy you can call 112 or the 1515 line of the Carabinieri Forestali (environmental police).
  • Only move the animal if you have to, and do it gently so you don't make any injuries worse.

Get the microchip scanned: the fastest route to the owner

Nearly all dogs (and many cats) have a microchip, a tiny device under the skin linked to a national pet registry that traces back to the owner. It's the most direct way to solve the whole thing in a few hours.

  • Take the animal (or have it scanned) at a vet, the local public veterinary service or a municipal shelter: reading the microchip is free and painless.
  • The chip number lets the registry identify the registered owner and get in touch.
  • No microchip? Don't lose heart: the next steps cover other ways to reunite them.

Notify the local shelter: in Italy it's the law

In Italy, whoever finds a stray animal is legally required to report it. This isn't pointless paperwork: it's often exactly how the owner gets their animal back.

  • Report the find to the municipal shelter or the local public veterinary service.
  • An official report starts the proper checks and keeps you on the right side of the rules.
  • Don't keep the animal secretly: beyond being against the rules, it cuts off the owner's chance to find it through official channels.

Post a "found" report on Orma, with a photo and location

Official reports matter, but it's often the local grapevine that makes the difference. On Orma you can post a found or simply sighted animal in a few taps, so whoever lost it recognises it at a glance from the photo and the place.

  • Add a clear photo and mark where you saw it: it takes just a few seconds.
  • People who are near you get an automatic alert when you post, so the news reaches the right area straight away.
  • If the owner had already reported the animal with its microchip number, Orma can automatically match the lost and found reports.
  • You get in touch through the secure in-app chat: your contact details stay protected, and the animal's location on the map is deliberately blurred by about 150 metres to keep everyone safe.

In the meantime: what to do (and what not to)

While you wait for someone to come forward, there's still plenty you can do, always with common sense.

  • Ask around the neighbourhood and in nearby shops: the owner often lives just steps away.
  • Keep the animal warm, with water and a little suitable food, without overdoing it.
  • Don't promise or accept money: stay focused on getting it home.
  • If you can't keep it, the municipal shelter and public veterinary service are the right places to turn to.

Finding the way home is almost always a matter of a few hours and a few people passing the word along. You've done the hardest part by stopping to help: follow these steps calmly and you'll give that animal the best chance of getting back to its family. Thank you for being there.

faqEn.q: I found a dog with no owner, who should I call?
faqEn.a: If the dog seems healthy, contact your local council or municipal police, who arrange recovery through the local shelter or veterinary health service. If it's injured or in danger, call the emergency number (112 in Italy). With Orma you can also report it as found or sighted in a few taps, so nearby people get the alert.

faqEn.q: How can I tell if a found animal has a microchip?
faqEn.a: A microchip is read with a special scanner, available at vets, veterinary health services, and shelters. Bringing the animal there lets them trace the owner through the pet registry. On Orma, reporting a found animal can trigger an automatic microchip match with a lost-pet report.

faqEn.q: Can I keep a cat or dog I found?
faqEn.a: Not right away: the animal may have an owner searching for it. Report it to the authorities (council, veterinary health service, or shelter) and have the microchip checked. If no one claims it after the period set by law, fostering or adoption can be considered.

faqEn.q: I found an injured animal, what should I do first?
faqEn.a: If it's in danger or hurt, call the emergency number (112 in Italy), or the forest rangers for wildlife. Avoid handling it if you might get hurt or make things worse, and try to get it to a vet. Meanwhile you can report it on Orma to alert people nearby.

en.title: Pet Microchip: Why It's Decisive for Reuniting You With a Lost Pet
en.metaDesc: A pet microchip is the safest way to be reunited with a lost pet. Learn how the registry works, how to keep your details current, and how Orma helps.
en.html:
When a pet goes missing, the first hours feel endless and the mind races. In moments like these, a pet microchip makes a real difference: it's a tiny device that links your dog or cat to your name and contact details. A vet or shelter that finds your animal can read the chip and trace it back to you. That's why the microchip is, today, the most reliable tool for bringing a friend home. This guide explains in plain language what it is, how the animal registry works, and what to do to keep everything in order so a microchip lost pet can actually find its way back.

What a Microchip Is and How the Registry Works

A microchip is a small glass cylinder about the size of a grain of rice, placed under the skin at the side of the neck. It has no battery and sends out no signal: it simply holds a unique identification number. That number is stored in an official animal registry a database that links the code to you as the owner.

The key thing to understand is this: the chip on its own doesn't say who you are. It works because the code is connected to an up-to-date record with your contact details. If your details are correct, whoever reads the chip can reach you. If they're outdated, the code stays just a number.

Legally Required for Dogs, Strongly Advised for Cats

In Italy, microchipping is legally required for all dogs: the chip must be implanted and registered, usually within the first months of life and before any transfer or adoption. It isn't a mere formality it's the foundation for identifying an animal and fighting abandonment.

For cats, the requirement varies by region, but a microchip is strongly recommended everywhere. Cats wander easily, often without a collar, and without a chip they're nearly impossible to return to their owner. If your cat goes outside or could simply slip out of a window a microchip is your most important safety net.

How a Microchip Is Read: Who Can Do It

Reading a microchip is quick and free. It takes a dedicated scanner, which is normally available at:

  • any veterinary practice or clinic;
  • shelters and municipal pounds;
  • the local public veterinary service (in Italy, the ASL);
  • often animal welfare associations and some authorities too.

If you find an animal, the most helpful thing you can do is take it or report it to one of these points so they can scan the chip. If you believe an animal is in danger or being mistreated, in Italy you can call 112 or the forestry police on 1515.

How to Keep Your Registry Details Current

A microchip only truly helps if the linked details are current. It's the step almost everyone forgets. Here's a checklist to run through:

  • Phone number and address: update them whenever you move or change your number.
  • Change of ownership: if you adopt or rehome an animal, the transfer must be recorded in the registry a private agreement isn't enough.
  • Yearly check: once a year, ask your vet to scan the chip and confirm your details are correct.
  • Where to update: registrations and changes are handled through the local public veterinary service or an authorized vet in your region.

It takes five minutes and spares you the worst outcome: a found animal that no one can connect back to you.

How Orma Uses the Microchip for Automatic Matching

Even with a perfectly registered chip, there are still hours when your animal is out there and no one has yet brought it to a vet. This is where Orma comes in, the community app for lost pets. When you report your animal as missing and enter its microchip number, the app automatically compares it with reports of found animals: if someone reports an animal with that code, automatic microchip matching connects you right away.

Around this, Orma automatically alerts people near where your pet went missing, gathers sightings with photos and location, and protects your contacts with a secure in-app chat. Animals' positions on the map are blurred by around 150 metres to protect privacy. You can get started here and keep your pets' profiles ready before you ever need them.

A microchip isn't a magic guarantee, but it's the most solid way we have today to reunite an animal with its owner. If your dog or cat is already registered, take a moment to check that your details are current. If it isn't yet, talk to your vet: it's a small step that, in the hardest moment, can make all the difference.

faqEn.q: Does a pet microchip have GPS to locate a lost dog?
faqEn.a: No, a microchip has no GPS and does not track location. It's a small passive transponder that, when scanned with a reader, shows a code linked to your details in the national pet registry: it identifies the animal and points back to you, it doesn't follow it on a map.

faqEn.q: Who can scan the microchip of a found dog or cat?
faqEn.a: Vets, shelters and public veterinary services have the scanner and can read a microchip for free. If you find an animal, take it or report it to one of these places: from the code they can trace the owner through the registry.

faqEn.q: What should I do if I changed my phone number or address?
faqEn.a: Update your contact details in the pet registry right away, usually through your vet or the local public veterinary service. A microchip linked to an old number makes it hard for whoever finds your pet to reach you.

faqEn.q: Is a microchip mandatory for cats too?
faqEn.a: In Italy the microchip is mandatory for dogs; for cats it depends on the region and is becoming increasingly common. Either way it's strongly recommended for every pet: it's the most reliable way to reunite a lost animal with its owner.

en.title: How to Adopt a Dog or Cat from a Shelter: A Simple Guide
en.metaDesc: Thinking of adopting a dog or a cat from a shelter? A calm, practical guide to shelter adoption: how it works, what to consider, and how to find rescues near you.
en.html:
Choosing to adopt a dog or adopt a cat from a shelter means giving a home to an animal who doesn't have one, instead of buying. It's a wonderful decision, but one to make calmly and thoughtfully: a pet becomes part of the family for many years. This guide walks you through how shelter adoption works, what to weigh up before you say yes, and how to spot the listings you should stay away from.

Why adopt from a shelter instead of buying

Shelters and rescues are full of dogs and cats waiting for a family. When you adopt a dog or adopt a cat from a shelter, you don't just help one animal: you free up a space so another one can be taken in. In practice, you save two lives at once.

  • You give a second chance to an animal who has often already lived through being abandoned.
  • You don't fuel puppy mills or irregular breeding.
  • Many shelter animals are already adults, so you know their character and size from the start.
  • Adoptions are usually free or ask for a small contribution, and the animal typically comes already vet-checked, vaccinated and microchipped.

How shelter adoption works, step by step

Adopting a dog or a cat from a shelter is straightforward, but it always involves getting to know each other first: you don't take an animal home at first sight. Here are the most common steps.

  • Visit the shelter or rescue. Book a time, look around without rushing, and ask the staff or volunteers about the animals' stories.
  • Get to know the animal. Meet more than once: watch how they react to you, to your family and to other animals. Ask about temperament, habits and any health needs.
  • Fill in the adoption application. The shelter may ask about your home and routine. That's normal, it helps them find the right match.
  • Sign the adoption agreement. You'll receive a form committing you to care for the animal, and the microchip is registered in your name in the official pet database.
  • Prepare for the homecoming. Many rescues do a follow-up in the weeks after, even just a phone call, to check that everything is going well.

What to consider before you adopt

Before you adopt from a shelter, pause and ask yourself honestly whether it's the right time. It's kinder to say no now than to return an animal after a few weeks.

  • Time. Dogs need daily walks and company; cats need attention too. Who will be with them during the day?
  • Space and lifestyle. Small flat, garden, working hours, travel: choose a size and character that fit your real life, not an idealised one.
  • Costs. Budget for food, vet visits, yearly vaccinations, parasite treatments and the occasional surprise. A pet is an ongoing expense.
  • Family. Children, other pets, possible allergies: talk it through with everyone first, because the choice should be shared.
  • The long haul. A dog or cat can live 15 years or more. It's a long commitment, not a spur-of-the-moment decision.

Watch out for suspicious listings

Alongside genuine adoptions, there are scams and unclear rehoming offers, especially online. A few warning signs worth knowing.

  • They ask for money upfront for "transport" or "paperwork" before you've even seen the animal.
  • They give away purebred puppies "urgently", with no microchip or health records.
  • They won't let you visit where the animal lives, or avoid meeting in person.
  • They sign nothing and disappear after handing the animal over.

Always prefer recognised shelters, rescues and associations. Ask to see the microchip and documents, and have your new companion checked by a trusted vet after adoption. If you suspect animal cruelty or trafficking, in Italy you can alert the environmental police (Carabinieri Forestali) on 1515 or call 112.

How Orma helps you find adoptions near you

Finding the right shelter isn't always easy. With Orma you can see adoptions from shelters and rescues near you, with photos and a description of each animal, so you can get a sense of them before you even visit.

  • Browse the dogs and cats looking for a home calmly, with no pressure.
  • Contact the shelter safely from the app, with your details kept private.
  • Arrive at your appointment already informed, with a clearer idea of who you might meet.

Adopting changes a life, and often yours too. Take the time you need, ask the right questions, and choose with your heart but also with your head: when the moment comes, you'll know the right animal for you.

faqEn.q: How much does it cost to adopt a dog or cat from a shelter?
faqEn.a: Adopting from a public shelter is usually free or requires a small contribution. Many shelters hand over the animal already microchipped, vaccinated and neutered, so ask about any fees before you go.

faqEn.q: What do I need to adopt a dog from a shelter?
faqEn.a: Usually an ID document and a signed adoption form are enough. Some shelters also hold a short interview or a home check to make sure the environment suits the animal.

faqEn.q: Can I adopt a dog if I work all day?
faqEn.a: It depends on the dog: some cope well with hours alone, others struggle. Talk to the shelter staff, who know each animal's temperament and can point you to one that fits your routine.

faqEn.q: Is it better to adopt a puppy or an adult dog from a shelter?
faqEn.a: A puppy needs more time for training and socialisation, while an adult often has a settled, more predictable character. There's no single right choice: weigh the time and experience you have.

en.title: Dog ran away from fireworks: what to do
en.metaDesc: Your dog ran away from the fireworks on New Year's Eve? Here's what to do right away, where a scared dog hides and how to bring him home calmly.
en.html:
If your dog ran away because of the fireworks on New Year's Eve, take a breath: what you feel right now, so many people have felt too, and most dogs do come home. A scared dog runs from fireworks not because he wants to leave you, but because the noise terrifies him and his instinct tells him only one thing: run far from the danger. This guide gives you calm, concrete steps to follow right away, without letting panic take over.

Why dogs run away from loud noise

Fireworks are sudden, very loud and impossible to predict. To a dog they feel like explosions with no explanation: the body goes into alarm and the flight instinct kicks in. A frightened dog often snaps the leash, jumps a fence or bolts through an open door, and in those minutes he no longer responds to your call. It isn't disobedience, it's pure fear. Understanding this helps you search the right way, without chasing and shouting, which would only scare him more.

Act right away, despite the chaos

Even if it's night and everything is confusing, the first minutes matter. Move calmly, but don't wait.

  • Call his name in a soft, steady voice, not a shout: a calm tone reassures him.
  • Don't chase him at a run. If you see him, crouch down, avoid sudden moves and offer a treat or his food bowl.
  • Alert family, neighbours and friends nearby, so many eyes are looking at once.
  • Get a recent photo ready and note any distinctive marks: you'll need them for the report.

Where scared dogs hide

A dog gripped by fear tends to go far away, much farther than you'd expect, and to hide in quiet places. He may cover several kilometres before stopping, disoriented and lost.

  • Check quiet, sheltered spots: bushes, garages, courtyards, under stairs, fields at the edge of town.
  • Search along natural escape routes, away from the noise of the fireworks.
  • Bring something that smells of home and his harness.
  • Ask everyone you meet whether they saw a frightened dog run past.

Let him find his way back to you

Many dogs, once the panic fades, retrace their steps toward home. Help him find you through his sense of smell.

  • Leave the gate or door open, if you can do so safely.
  • Put out a blanket with his scent, his bed, and bowls of water and food.
  • Don't wash his blanket right away: the familiar smell is a powerful call.
  • Leave a small light on and stay reachable, so anyone who finds him can contact you.

Search when the fireworks stop

The best time to search is when silence returns, usually late at night or at dawn. In the quiet, many dogs come out of hiding and let you get close.

  • Go out in the calm hours, move slowly and speak in a low voice.
  • The next day, alert local shelters, rescue centres and vets: a found dog is often taken there.
  • Contact the local veterinary health service (in Italy, the ASL): if the dog has a microchip, scanning it traces him back to you through the pet registry.
  • If the dog is in danger (on a busy road, injured or unreachable) you can call the emergency services (in Italy, 112, or 1515 for the Forestry Carabinieri).

Report it on Orma and alert your neighbours

In frightening moments, many people searching together make the difference. With Orma you can report your lost dog in a few taps and alert people nearby. Anyone who spots him can send you a photo and the location, and if someone takes him to a vet, automatic microchip matching helps reunite you. You can also generate a flyer with a QR code to print and put up around your area. The map shows the location approximately to protect your privacy.

Preventing it next year

Once it's all over, a few simple habits can spare you another scare next New Year's Eve.

  • Don't leave your dog alone during fireworks: your presence calms him.
  • Set up a quiet refuge at home, with his bed and background sound to soften the bangs.
  • Keep his microchip and your contact details up to date in the registry.
  • If he's very sensitive to noise, talk to your vet well in advance.

Searching for a runaway dog at night is frightening, we know. But keep going gently: many four-legged friends come home in the hours that follow, as soon as the noise stops. Keep looking, keep the right channels open, and let his instinct guide him back to you.

faqEn.q: My dog ran away from the fireworks, will he come home on his own?
faqEn.a: Many dogs return on their own once the panic settles, often late at night or at dawn. Leave the gate open and put out a blanket with his scent and his bowl to help him find his way back.

faqEn.q: How far can a dog scared by fireworks travel?
faqEn.a: A terrified dog can run for several kilometres before stopping, disoriented. Extend your search beyond the neighbourhood and check quiet, sheltered places.

faqEn.q: What should I do if I can't find my dog on New Year's Eve?
faqEn.a: Try again during the quiet hours, then the next day alert local shelters, rescue centres and vets, and the veterinary health service. Report the loss on Orma to alert people nearby.

faqEn.q: Does a microchip help find a runaway dog?
faqEn.a: Yes. If someone takes the dog to a vet or shelter, scanning the microchip traces him back to you through the pet registry, as long as your details are up to date.

en.title: How to Make a Lost Pet Poster That Actually Works
en.metaDesc: A calm, practical guide to a lost dog flyer: what to write, the right photo, where to post it, and mistakes to avoid. Plus a ready PDF poster with QR from Orma.
en.html:
When a pet goes missing, every minute feels endless and your mind races in every direction. A good lost pet poster is one of the simplest and most powerful tools you have: it speaks to your neighbourhood even while you're somewhere else. You don't need any design skills. You need clarity. In this guide we'll calmly go through how to make a lost dog flyer that truly works, what it should include, where to post it, and which mistakes to avoid.

What a lost pet poster must include

A lost pet poster is read in just a few seconds, often from a distance or from a passing car. So it has to say the essentials right away. Here's what it can't miss:

  • One large, sharp photo: the face and coat should be clearly visible. One photo filling half the page beats many small ones.
  • The word LOST or MISSING, big and clear: large, near the top, so anyone glancing at it instantly understands.
  • Area and date: the neighbourhood or street and the day it happened help people connect a sighting.
  • A simple contact: one large, easy-to-read phone number. Just one, the one you'll always answer.
  • The line "Please don't chase, call me": a frightened pet runs if chased. Asking people not to chase and to call you instead raises your chances of getting them back.

The right photo makes the difference

The photo is what stops the eye. Choose one where your pet is easy to recognise: in daylight, in focus, with true colours. If they have a distinctive mark (a patch, a collar, a folded ear), a photo that shows it is ideal. Avoid dark, blurry, or from-behind shots.

Where to post the flyer

A perfect flyer in the wrong spot does little. Focus on places where local people pass by:

  • The exact spot where your pet vanished and the surrounding streets: that's where someone may have seen them.
  • Vets, clinics and pet shops: people who work with animals are the most likely to notice a sighting.
  • Cafés, bakeries, newsstands and small shops: kindly ask to display it near the till.
  • Schools, parks and community boards: lots of different people pass through every day.

If you can, laminate the sheets or slip them into a clear plastic sleeve so they survive the rain.

Mistakes to avoid

Many flyers fail over small details. The most common ones:

  • Too much text: long paragraphs go unread. A few big words work better.
  • A small or unclear photo: if your pet isn't recognisable, the flyer loses its power.
  • No contact, or a tiny number: without an easy way to reach you, whoever finds them won't know what to do.
  • Faded black and white: print the photo in colour if you can.

A ready poster in one tap with Orma

Putting it all together by hand, with photo and QR code, can feel like a lot in an already hard moment. That's why Orma generates a ready-made PDF poster straight from your report: a large photo, the key details, and a QR code that anyone can scan to see the up-to-date listing and contact you. Download it, print it, post it, all in minutes. In the same Orma app you can also alert nearby people and receive sightings with photo and location, while the map shows an approximate position (about 150 metres) to protect your privacy.

Take a breath. A clear flyer, posted in the right places, puts many people to work alongside you. In the meantime, notify your local shelter and vet services and check that your pet's microchip is properly registered: small steps that often make the difference. Many pets find their way home thanks to a neighbour who spotted the right flyer at the right moment.

faqEn.q: What information should a lost dog flyer include?
faqEn.a: The word LOST clearly visible, one large sharp photo, the area and date your pet went missing, a big phone number, and the line "please don't chase, call me." Keep it short and clear.

faqEn.q: Where should I put up a lost pet poster?
faqEn.a: At the spot where your pet vanished and nearby streets, at vets and pet shops, in cafés, newsstands and small shops, and on community boards, in parks and near schools. Laminate it to survive the rain.

faqEn.q: How can I make a flyer if I can't use design software?
faqEn.a: The Orma app generates a ready-made PDF poster from your report, with a large photo and a QR code. You just download it, print it, and post it in minutes.

faqEn.q: What else should I do besides the flyer if my pet is lost?
faqEn.a: Notify your local shelter and vet services, check that the microchip is properly registered, and report the loss on Orma to alert nearby people. If an animal is in danger in Italy, call 112 or the Forestry Carabinieri on 1515.

en.title: Lost pets beyond cats and dogs: how to find rabbits, birds, rodents and ferrets
en.metaDesc: Lost rabbit, escaped parrot or missing ferret? A calm, practical guide to searching each species the right way. They need you just as much.
en.html:
When a rabbit, a parrot, a small rodent or a ferret goes missing, the empty feeling at home is exactly the same as losing a cat or a dog. Yet people often freeze, unsure where to start, because these animals move and hide in very different ways. The good news is that once you understand their habits, your chances of finding them go up a lot. And remember: Orma is made for every animal, not just cats and dogs. Take a breath, and let's go one step at a time.

Birds and parrots: look up and stay local

An escaped parrot or a lost pet bird rarely flies far right away. In the first days it tends to stay in the same area, often perched high in trees or on rooftops. Always look up: many people search the ground and miss it completely.

  • Go out at dawn, when birds are most active and vocal, and listen for its call among the trees.
  • Place its open cage outside, on the balcony or in the garden, with food and water: the pull of the "safe place" often works.
  • If you have another bird companion, bring it close; its calls can draw the escaped one back.
  • Play familiar sounds, like your voice or a whistle it knows, moving calmly and slowly.

Rabbits and rodents: they hide nearby, in dark, tight spots

A lost rabbit or a small escaped rodent almost never travels far. They are crepuscular animals and prey by nature: their instinct is to hide, not to run. Search close to home, in dark and narrow gaps.

  • Check under hedges, wood piles, parked cars, pipes, stairs and sheds: look for the tightest spaces.
  • Search at dawn and dusk, the times they are most likely to move around to eat.
  • Use food as a lure: fresh vegetables, a little hay or its favourite treat left in a quiet spot.
  • Move quietly and avoid sudden gestures: rushing and noise make them freeze even more.

Ferrets: search low, in holes and pipes

A lost ferret follows its nature: it slips into any gap it can find. It rarely climbs high and almost always stays low and close to where it disappeared.

  • Inspect pipes, drains, holes in the ground, wall cavities, garages and cellars.
  • Search at ground level, moving slowly and checking every crack.
  • Ask neighbours to check garages, sheds and basements: a ferret can enter through surprisingly small gaps.

Alert neighbours and vets, including exotics

For all these species, local word of mouth is incredibly powerful. Whoever finds them often doesn't know who to turn to.

  • Talk to neighbours and nearby shops: many sightings come straight from them.
  • Notify nearby vets, including those specialised in exotic animals, where someone might bring the animal they found.
  • Contact your local shelter or rescue and the veterinary services: small animals can end up there too.
  • With Orma you can report a lost pet in a few taps and alert people nearby, who receive your report with photo and location.

How Orma helps with every animal

Orma makes no distinction by species: the community is here for your rabbit, your parrot or your ferret just as much as for a dog or a cat.

  • You report the lost pet and people nearby get an alert: more eyes searching for you.
  • Anyone who spots your animal can send you a sighting with photo and location, through the secure in-app chat.
  • The map shows a blurred location of about 150 metres, so your privacy stays protected.
  • You can create a PDF flyer with a QR code straight from the app, to print and put up around the neighbourhood.

Searching for a less common pet takes patience and a bit of strategy, but so many families find their rabbit, their little bird or their ferret exactly this way. Learn its habits, involve your neighbours and let the community do its part. Every animal matters, and yours deserves to come home too.

faqEn.q: My rabbit is lost, where should I look first?
faqEn.a: Search close to home, in dark and tight spots like hedges, wood piles and under cars. Rabbits hide rather than run, and come out more readily at dawn and dusk.

faqEn.q: My parrot escaped from home, will it come back on its own?
faqEn.a: It often stays in the area for the first few days, perched high in trees. Put its open cage outside with food and search at dawn, when it is most active and vocal.

faqEn.q: How do I search for a lost ferret?
faqEn.a: Look low and nearby: ferrets slip into holes, pipes, garages and cellars. Ask neighbours to check the tight spaces where it might be hiding.

faqEn.q: Can I use Orma for pets other than cats and dogs?
faqEn.a: Yes. Orma is made for every animal: you can report a lost pet, receive sightings with photo and location, and alert people nearby, whatever the species.

en.title: How to Trap a Lost Cat Safely: A Calm, Patient Guide
en.metaDesc: A scared cat won't let you grab it and shouldn't be chased. Learn how to use food, routine and a humane trap to bring your cat home calmly.
en.html:
When a cat goes missing, your heart races and you want to search everywhere at once. But a frightened cat behaves differently from what we expect: it hides, stays still and often won't even respond to its own name. It's not that it doesn't recognise you, it's that fear freezes it. That's why learning how to trap a lost cat the right way is mostly about patience and never chasing. This guide gives you gentle, concrete steps to bring your cat home.

Why a scared cat won't let you catch it

A cat in trouble goes into survival mode. Even the most affectionate pet, lost and disoriented outside, may not let anyone approach, not even you. Chasing, calling loudly or trying to grab it only pushes it further away.

  • Don't run towards it or make sudden movements.
  • Crouch down, speak softly and let the cat come to you.
  • If you spot it hiding, mark the place and return calmly, ideally at dawn or dusk.

Build a routine with food at fixed times

The most effective way to bring a cat back is to become predictable to it. Put tasty food (wet food or tuna) in the same spot at the same time every day, usually in the evening. The cat will learn to trust that place and pass by regularly.

  • Choose a quiet, sheltered spot near where it was last seen.
  • Add a worn t-shirt of yours or its blanket: familiar smells are reassuring.
  • Don't move the feeding spot: consistency matters more than quantity.

Use a trail camera to learn when it passes

Before trying to catch it, it helps to know if and when the cat actually shows up. A small trail camera or a camera pointed at the bowl tells you what time it passes and whether it's really your cat. This saves you wasted attempts and lets you act at the right moment.

  • Check the footage each morning without lingering at the spot.
  • Note the times: you'll need them to set the trap.

How a humane trap works

A humane cat trap is a cage that closes gently when the animal steps in for food, without hurting it. It's the safest tool for how to catch a scared cat without chasing. You can often borrow one.

  • Borrow a trap from cat rescues, volunteer groups, shelters or your local vet.
  • Place it at the feeding spot only once you know the cat passes by.
  • Cover the cage with a cloth: to the cat it will look like a safe shelter.
  • Never leave it unattended for long: check it often, even from a distance.

Patience, silence and the right timing

Trapping can take days. That's normal. Stay quiet, keep your distance and don't give up if nothing happens the first few nights: you're building trust. Many cats come back precisely because someone kept leaving food and didn't stop.

  • Avoid noise, dogs and people around the trap.
  • In cold or rain, think carefully about timing and shelter.

As soon as it's caught: see the vet for the microchip

The moment the cat is safe inside the trap, take it to a vet to read the microchip and check it's well. If it's yours, you can confirm its identity; if it belongs to someone else, the microchip helps trace the family through the pet registry. With Orma you can report the lost cat and receive sightings from people nearby, so you know where to focus your food and trap. You can also generate a flyer with a QR code to print for your neighbourhood.

Getting a cat back is almost always about calm rather than speed. Trust the routine, respect its pace and surround yourself with people who can help: rescues, volunteers and neighbours often make the difference. With a little patience, that bowl you leave out every evening can be the thread that guides your friend home.

faqEn.q: How long does it take to trap a lost cat?
faqEn.a: It can take from a few days to a couple of weeks. It depends on how scared the cat is and how consistently you leave food and the trap in the same spot at the same time.

faqEn.q: Where can I borrow a humane cat trap?
faqEn.a: You can ask cat rescues, volunteer groups, shelters or your local vet. Many local organisations lend them for free to people looking for a lost cat.

faqEn.q: What should I do as soon as I catch the cat?
faqEn.a: Take it straight to a vet to read the microchip and check it's healthy. The microchip lets you trace the family through the pet registry.

faqEn.q: Should I chase the cat if I see it?
faqEn.a: No. Chasing or calling loudly scares it and makes it run further away. It's better to mark the spot, stay calm and leave food in the same place every evening.

en.title: Dog Missing for Days: What to Do to Find Them
en.metaDesc: Your dog hasn't come home for days or even a week? A calm, practical guide to keep searching without losing hope. Real advice for Italy with Orma.
en.html:
If your dog has been missing for days, we know how hard every passing hour feels. First, we want you to hear this: it isn't over. Many lost dogs are found even after a week or more, sometimes far from home. The fear of not finding them is natural, but right now what matters most is to keep searching with a clear method and steady patience. In this guide you'll find concrete steps to leave nothing untried, calmly and one at a time.

Don't lose hope: dogs come back even after weeks

A dog who hasn't come home is not a dog lost forever. Many animals wander off, get frightened, hide, and are then spotted or recovered days later. The most important thing is to stay present in the search: people who give up too soon sometimes stop right when their dog is about to be found.

  • Keep your phone reachable at all times, even at night.
  • Keep walking the area during quiet hours, at dawn and dusk, when frightened dogs move most.
  • Bring something that smells of home or their favourite food.

Widen your search area, little by little

As the days go by, a dog can travel a long way. If you first searched close to home, now is the time to expand the area gradually, without rushing and in an orderly way.

  • Widen the search circle each day, adding neighbourhoods, country roads and nearby green areas.
  • Ask people who live or work in the area: postal workers, couriers, farmers, other dog walkers.
  • On Orma you can update your location and alert nearby people as you move around.

Recontact shelters and the local vet service every few days

Shelters and public veterinary services take in new animals all the time. A round of calls made last week may already be out of date, so it's important to check back regularly.

  • Call your local shelter and public veterinary service every few days, not just once.
  • Check their websites and social pages: many places post photos of animals as soon as they arrive.
  • Make sure your dog's microchip is registered with your up-to-date contact details, so a shelter can trace them back to you.

Refresh your flyers and posts

Over time flyers get damaged, covered up or forgotten. Tidying them up and sharing them again helps keep people's attention alive.

  • Replace torn or faded flyers and put up new ones in the areas where you've widened the search.
  • From the app you can generate a PDF flyer with a QR code, ready to print and share.
  • Repost your notice in local groups and ask shops, cafés and vets to display it again.

Keep your Orma report active and up to date

A report left untouched risks going unnoticed. Keeping it active and current improves the chance that someone connects a sighting to your dog.

  • Update the report with the latest area you've searched and with clear, recent photos.
  • Check nearby sightings every day and reply in the chat calmly.
  • If your dog is microchipped, automatic matching can alert you when someone reports a compatible found dog.

If someone finds or spots them

People who come across a lost dog don't always know what to do. A few clear pointers can make the difference.

  • Anyone who finds a dog can take them to a vet or the local veterinary service for a free microchip scan.
  • If an animal is in danger on the road, or in case of suspected mistreatment, in Italy you can call 112 or 1515 (Carabinieri Forestali).
  • Invite whoever spots them to report it on Orma with a photo and location, so the alert reaches you right away.

We know these days are heavy. Keep searching steadily, lean on the people around you, and don't stop believing: every day that passes is also one more day when someone may have seen them. Many families have held their dog again just when they feared the worst. One step at a time, you're on the right path.

faqEn.q: My dog has been missing for a week, can I still find them?
faqEn.a: Yes. Many dogs are found even after a week or more, sometimes far from home. Keep searching, widen your area, and recontact shelters and the local vet service regularly.

faqEn.q: How often should I call the shelter and vet service?
faqEn.a: Every few days, not just once, because new animals arrive all the time. Also check their websites and social pages, where they often post photos of new arrivals.

faqEn.q: Why does the microchip matter if my dog is missing?
faqEn.a: If the microchip is registered with your up-to-date contact details, a vet or shelter can trace it back to you. On Orma it can also trigger an automatic match with a found dog.

faqEn.q: What can someone who finds my dog do?
faqEn.a: They can take them to a vet or the local veterinary service for a free microchip scan and report them on Orma with a photo and location. If the animal is in danger or mistreatment is suspected, in Italy you can call 112 or 1515.

en.title: Pet Lost on Holiday or in Summer: What to Do
en.metaDesc: Dog lost on holiday or pet lost while traveling? Here's what to do right away, step by step, to find your animal wherever you are in Italy.
en.html:
Being far from home and suddenly not seeing your dog or cat anywhere is one of the most frightening moments a pet owner can face. Your heart races, it's hard to think clearly, and you don't know where to start. Take a breath: there are concrete steps you can follow right now, even in a place you don't know. This guide walks you through them calmly, one at a time.

Why the risk goes up in summer and on holiday

On holiday your pet is in an unfamiliar place, without the landmarks of home. A sudden noise or an open gate is enough for it to bolt in any direction, with no idea how to get back.

  • Summer thunderstorms and holiday fireworks scare many dogs, who run off in a panic.
  • Holiday homes, campsites and beaches are open, unfamiliar spaces.
  • By the sea or in the mountains, the smells and routes your pet knows are missing, so it struggles to find its way home.

Act right away where you are, not back home

The most common mistake is searching near your house. But a dog lost on holiday is where you lost it: that's where the alerts need to reach.

  • Report the loss in the exact place where it disappeared, not in your home town.
  • With Orma you open a report in a few taps and automatically alert the people near you at that moment.
  • Go back to the exact spot where you last saw it: animals often stay nearby or return there.

Alert local shelters and vets

Whoever finds a lost animal usually takes it to the nearest vet or shelter. That's why you should contact the facilities in the holiday area.

  • Call the local public dog shelter and the veterinary service of the local health authority (ASL).
  • Stop by nearby veterinary clinics: they can scan the microchip of any animal brought in.
  • Leave everyone a recent photo and a phone number you can always be reached on.

An up-to-date microchip lets you be traced anywhere

The microchip is your strongest ally for a pet lost while traveling, far from home. Whoever scans it can trace you, in any region.

  • Before you leave, check that your details in the animal registry are up to date, especially your phone number.
  • With Orma, the automatic microchip matching connects whoever found an animal with whoever is looking for it.
  • A tag with your number on the collar helps a finder call you immediately, without needing a microchip scanner.

Use sightings, the map and the flyer

The more eyes on your side, the better. A pet lost while traveling is often found thanks to someone passing by who notices something.

  • Ask anyone who spots it to send a sighting with photo and location: this builds a trail of its movements.
  • The map with the location blurred by about 150 metres shows the area while protecting everyone's privacy.
  • Generate a PDF flyer with a QR code from the app to print and put up at the beach, in cafes and in local shops.
  • All of this works wherever you are in Italy, on Android and iPhone.

If you suspect abandonment or mistreatment

While searching you may come across situations that don't involve your pet but still deserve attention.

  • For emergencies and crimes against animals or the environment you can call 112 or the 1515 line of the Carabinieri Forestali.
  • Report calmly what you actually observed, without alarm.

Losing sight of your friend in an unfamiliar place is frightening, but you are not alone and it isn't all down to luck. By moving quickly in the right area, alerting local facilities and relying on the microchip and a community of people nearby, you genuinely improve the chances of holding your pet again. Orma guides you step by step, wherever you are.

faqEn.q: I lost my dog on holiday: should I report it where I live or where I lost it?
faqEn.a: Report it where you lost it. The people who can see or find it are in the holiday area, so that's where the alerts and flyers need to reach.

faqEn.q: Does the microchip help if I lost my pet far from home?
faqEn.a: Yes, a lot. Anyone who scans the microchip can trace you anywhere in Italy, as long as your registry details are up to date, especially your phone number.

faqEn.q: Who should I call if I find or lose an animal in a place I don't know?
faqEn.a: Contact the local public dog shelter and the veterinary service of the local health authority (ASL), and stop by nearby vet clinics to have the microchip scanned. For emergencies or suspected crimes you can call 112 or the 1515 line of the Carabinieri Forestali.

faqEn.q: Does Orma work even if I'm on holiday in another region?
faqEn.a: Yes. Orma works wherever you are in Italy: open a report at your current location and automatically alert the people nearby, on Android and iPhone.

en.title: Your Pet's Microchip Details Are Out of Date: What to Do (and Why It Matters)
en.metaDesc: A microchip with old details won't bring your pet home. Here's how to update your phone, address and owner info in the pet registry, calmly and in good time.
en.html:
If your dog or cat ever wanders off, a microchip can be the difference between a quick reunion and days of worry. But there's something many people don't realise: a chip only works if the details linked to it are correct. An old phone number or an address from two house moves ago can make a microchip almost useless. The good news is that fixing this is simple, and you can do it now, before any emergency.

Why a microchip with old details won't help find your pet

A microchip is a small device under the skin that holds a number code. On its own, that code says nothing: it points to a record in your national or regional pet registry, where your contact details are stored. If someone who finds your pet (a vet, a shelter, a kind stranger) scans the chip but reaches a disconnected number, the chain breaks at the very last step.

  • A changed phone number means nobody can call you.
  • An old address sends letters to the wrong place.
  • An outdated owner record (after an adoption or a gift) creates confusion about who to contact.

In short, taking a moment to update your pet's microchip details matters as much as having the chip fitted in the first place.

When to update your pet registry details

There are clear moments when it's worth pausing to check your pet's record. Update the details whenever:

  • you've changed your phone number or email;
  • you've moved home, even just to another neighbourhood;
  • there's been a change of microchip owner (adoption, a gift, inheritance).

Don't wait until you "need" it: the right time to fix your details is now, while everything is calm. A five-minute check today can save you hours of frantic searching tomorrow.

How to update the microchip: practical steps

Registries are run at a national or regional level, so the exact process can vary, but the essentials are the same. Here's how to go about it:

  • Have the microchip number ready (you'll find it in your pet's health booklet or European passport) and a form of ID.
  • Contact the body that manages your pet registry. In Italy this is the veterinary service of your local health authority (ASL), or simply ask your trusted vet, who can often do the update for you.
  • Give the correct details: phone, address, email and, if needed, the new owner.
  • For a change of microchip owner, you'll usually need signatures from both the person handing over and the person receiving the animal; ask in advance which forms to bring.
  • Keep the receipt or confirmation of the update.

If you're not sure whether your pet is already registered, or with which details, the registry can check this using the chip number.

How Orma uses the microchip number for automatic matching

With Orma, the community app for lost pets in Italy, your microchip becomes even more useful. When you report your pet as lost and enter the chip number, the app compares it with reports of found animals: if someone has found a pet with the same code, automatic matching connects you through a secure in-app chat.

  • Report a lost, found or sighted animal in just a few taps.
  • People nearby get an alert and can help.
  • The map location is blurred by about 150 metres to protect privacy.
  • You can generate a PDF flyer with a QR code straight from the app.

The microchip number stays the common thread: the more up to date the linked details are, the better this tool works for you. You can start using Orma on Android and iPhone.

A small act that means a lot

Updating a microchip doesn't take much: one call to the registry or a visit to the vet, and your pet's record becomes genuinely useful again. It's one of those quiet tasks you do once and then stop worrying about. Take five minutes, check your details and, if anything has changed, sort it out today: your friend will never know, but you'll rest a little easier.

faqEn.q: How do I update my dog's microchip details?
faqEn.a: Contact the body that runs your pet registry (in Italy, the veterinary service of your local health authority, the ASL) or your trusted vet. Bring the microchip number and an ID, and give the correct phone, address and, if needed, the new owner.

faqEn.q: What do I need to change the microchip owner?
faqEn.a: You'll usually need the chip number, a form of ID, and signatures from both the previous and the new owner. Ask the registry or your vet in advance which forms to bring, as the process can vary by region.

faqEn.q: Should I update the microchip even if my pet isn't lost?
faqEn.a: Yes. It's best to do it in good time, right after a house move or a change of phone number. If your pet ever wanders off, up-to-date details let whoever finds them actually reach you.

faqEn.q: What is the microchip number used for in Orma?
faqEn.a: Orma uses the microchip number for automatic matching: if you report your pet as lost and someone reports a found animal with the same code, the app connects you through a secure in-app chat.
